hits.draft_en:
A new paper from Chinese researchers is titled "The End of Harness Engineering" - and agent frameworks should pay attention.

The claim: writing the code around the model by hand stops being a skill.

Why. A human-written harness is a single guess, for a single task, made on a single afternoon. It ships and then runs for months with nobody scoring it.

A loop-written harness grades itself instead:
- a small 4B model reviews what failed
- it suggests 8 edits
- the edit with the best score on held-out questions is the only one kept

The large model never changes. Every round only rebuilds the file that wraps it.

That leaves the human one job: curating the scoring set - the test questions used to grade each harness. Frameworks become disposable. Writing the exam becomes the work.

Claude Code just did the FBI's job in 3 minutes 52 seconds and traced $4.8 billion of NVIDIA chips to a 2-person company in Singapore. One of its execs turned out to be Jensen Huang's mistress.

It used 23 public sources. Four government probes have been working on this for over a year.

I gave it one question: where did the chips actually go?

It started with the New York Times and hit a paywall, 403. It didn't ask me what to do, it just switched to CBS and CNBC and kept reading.

The company is called Megaspeed. It was spun off from a Chinese gaming company in 2023 and had never run a data center. Then it started buying:

→ /purchases → $4.8B of NVIDIA chips in two years (CBS, NYT)
→ /math → $4.8B ÷ ~$35k per card ≈ 136,000 GPUs
→ /office → Singapore, 2 employees
→ /malaysia → 200+ shipments, about $2B in 12 months
→ /route → orders placed through a US reseller, never NVIDIA directly
→ /china → a server company in the chain moving hardware back into China
→ /site_visit → US inspectors found the GPUs still sealed in their boxes

136,000 of the most wanted chips on the planet, and nobody had even opened them.

Then it noticed two numbers that didn't match: $2B in one report, $4.8B in another. Claude checked the dates. The $2B was only the Malaysia route over 12 months, so the real total was the bigger one.

After that it found this:

→ a US intel memo says a Megaspeed exec was recruited by Chinese intelligence (TechCrunch, CBS)
→ according to the memo, her target was the man who decides where NVIDIA's chips go
→ Nov 8: Jensen Huang tells staff he had an affair with her (CNBC)
→ the same day, NVIDIA's board opens an independent investigation
→ 4 probes open: US Senate, Singapore police, US Commerce, and Bain pulled out as a tenant
→ Nov 18: the House wants a closed-door briefing

I stopped it halfway and asked: wait, didn't NVIDIA say this was debunked?

It went back and checked. On Oct 29 NVIDIA did call the diversion claims "debunked". Ten days later its own board opened an investigation into its own CEO.

At the end it built the whole map, 19 links, and wouldn't draw a single one without a source behind it.

Four probes in two countries have been at this for over a year. Claude Code finished before my coffee got cold.

Nobody has published where the 136,000 GPUs are now.

Save this.

Claude Code just did the FBI's job in 3 minutes 52 seconds and traced $4.8 billion of NVIDIA chips to a 2-person company in Singapore. One of its execs turned out to be Jensen Huang's mistress.

It used 23 public sources. Four government probes have been working on this for over a year.

I gave it one question: where did the chips actually go?

It started with the New York Times and hit a paywall, 403. It didn't ask me what to do, it just switched to CBS and CNBC and kept reading.

The company is called Megaspeed. It was spun off from a Chinese gaming company in 2023 and had never run a data center. Then it started buying:

→ /purchases → $4.8B of NVIDIA chips in two years (CBS, NYT)
→ /math → $4.8B ÷ ~$35k per card ≈ 136,000 GPUs
→ /office → Singapore, 2 employees
→ /malaysia → 200+ shipments, about $2B in 12 months
→ /route → orders placed through a US reseller, never NVIDIA directly
→ /china → a server company in the chain moving hardware back into China
→ /site_visit → US inspectors found the GPUs still sealed in their boxes

136,000 of the most wanted chips on the planet, and nobody had even opened them.

Then it noticed two numbers that didn't match: $2B in one report, $4.8B in another. Claude checked the dates. The $2B was only the Malaysia route over 12 months, so the real total was the bigger one.

After that it found this:

→ a US intel memo says a Megaspeed exec was recruited by Chinese intelligence (TechCrunch, CBS)
→ according to the memo, her target was the man who decides where NVIDIA's chips go
→ Nov 8: Jensen Huang tells staff he had an affair with her (CNBC)
→ the same day, NVIDIA's board opens an independent investigation
→ 4 probes open: US Senate, Singapore police, US Commerce, and Bain pulled out as a tenant
→ Nov 18: the House wants a closed-door briefing

I stopped it halfway and asked: wait, didn't NVIDIA say this was debunked?

It went back and checked. On Oct 29 NVIDIA did call the diversion claims "debunked". Ten days later its own board opened an investigation into its own CEO.

At the end it built the whole map, 19 links, and wouldn't draw a single one without a source behind it.

Four probes in two countries have been at this for over a year. Claude Code finished before my coffee got cold.

Nobody has published where the 136,000 GPUs are now.

Save this.

LLM provides intelligence.

virals.draft_en:
An AI agent is not just an LLM. It is a stack of five pieces, each with a job:

- LLM is the brain: it reads, writes, reasons and decides
- RAG is the library: it pulls in outside knowledge before the answer is written
- MCP is the nervous system: a standard protocol that wires the model to tools, apps and data
- Skills are muscle memory: reusable instructions and workflows so tasks come out the same way every time
- The agent is brain plus hands: reasoning, planning and tools working on their own

Put simply: intelligence from the LLM, knowledge from RAG, connectivity from MCP, repeatable abilities from skills. The agent ties them together and gets the work done.

- RAG is the library: it pulls in outside knowledge before the answer is written

1. Hit record (⌘⇧R or Ctrl+Shift+R) and do the task normally. You can talk through it out loud too.

3. GitHub Copilot turns the recording into a list of steps you can edit.
4. One click turns it into a skill your agent can run, or an automation on a schedule.

It generalizes from one example, so recording yourself submitting one form teaches the agent to submit all of them.
